slides.texte_overlay:
How to get what you want
without raising your voice
Ask clearly, with a number and a date. Not "Could you maybe help at some point?" but "Can you send it by Friday at noon?" Vague asks get vague answers. Clear asks get done.
Ask the person who can actually say yes. Not the receptionist, the manager. Not the group chat, the one friend who decides. Half of "no" comes from asking the wrong person.
Explain why it matters to them, not just to you. "If we fix this now, you won't get the angry calls next week." People say yes faster when they see what's in it for them.
Know your stuff before you ask. Five minutes a day of history, art or science sharpens how you think and argue. Calm, informed people get a yes far more often than loud ones.
slides.texte_sophia: I do five minutes a day on a micro-learning app like the Sophia app. History, art, science. It sharpened how I think and argue. Calm, informed people get a yes far more often.

slides.texte_overlay: Lower your voice when it gets tense. Slower, quieter, steady. It forces the other person to calm down to hear you, and the calmest person in a disagreement almost always wins it.
Be ready to hear no, and ask what would make it a yes. "Okay, what would need to change for this to work?" Most no's are really "not like this." That question turns them into a plan.
Follow up once, politely. "Just checking in on this." Most people never ask twice. A single calm reminder gets you what the first ask didn't, without anyone feeling pushed.
